$schema_note: Section-by-section index of Ramanujan's Quarterly Reports as reproduced in Berndt's 2022 Hardy-Ramanujan Journal paper (open-access reproduction of Satagopan 1925 handwritten copy).

source.title: Ramanujan's Quarterly Reports
source.based_on: Satagopan's 1925 handwritten copy of Ramanujan's three Quarterly Reports to the Board of Studies in Mathematics, University of Madras, dated 5 Aug 1913, 7 Nov 1913, 9 Mar 1914. Originals lost.

tagging_basis.tagging_method: hand-judgment, not regex; reading line-by-line through the Berndt reproduction
tagging_basis.method_note: Section-level granularity (one tag set per Ramanujan-numbered section), with operator detection at the level of the *mathematical move being executed*, not the surface-LaTeX notation. A section may carry multiple operator tags if it uses several moves.

extra_operators_taxonomy.purpose: Operators that DO appear in the QRs but are NOT in the predicted 6-operator schema. These are the empirical correction.

tags.definition: Fourier cosine (or sine) transform that is its own inverse up to a π/2 factor: F[f]=g implies F[g]=(π/2)f. Theorem III of QR II.
Extracting a sub-series f_k(x)=∑_{n≡k mod r} a_n x^n by averaging f(ω^j x) over r-th roots of unity ω. ChatGPT taxonomy approximates this with FINITE_GAUSS_COLLAPSE.
Taking the n→0 limit in a parametric Master-Theorem identity to land on ∫(φ(ax)-ψ(bx))/x dx-style formulas. Theorem II of QR II.
Defining F^n(x) for non-integer n via the Schröder-Koenig functional equation f^m = χ^{-1} ∘ φ ∘ χ. QR III §4-§6, §10.
Asymptotic comparison using Hardy's ≺ relation; constructing growth scales that defy logarithmic / exponential ones. QR III §7-§9.

Defining D^k for non-integer k via the Mellin-style integral ∫x^{n-1} f^{(r)}(a-x) dx = Γ(n) f^{(r-n)}(a). QR III §11. Mellin-adjacent but uses derivatives of f rather than the function itself; distinct operator move.
Substituting the shift operator E or difference operator Δ for a scalar parameter (a → E·D, etc.) in an identity that was proved for scalars. Heaviside-style. QR III §12.

Decomposing an infinite product 1/∏(1+x²/(a+k)²) into partial fractions in x² before integrating. QR III §13. ChatGPT taxonomy has PARTIAL_FRACTION_LATENTS for the moment-theory version; this is the multiplicative version.
Fourier-transform identity with a sharp cutoff at the bandwidth (π/2 below, π/4 at the cutoff, 0 above). QR III §14.
Reciprocal-function pair (F,f) defined by ∫x^{p-1} F(x) dx · ∫x^{-p} f(x) dx = π/sin(πp), generalizing Fourier self-reciprocity to arbitrary Mellin-pairs. QR III §15.

sections.title: Subject of the paper — statement of the Master Theorem
sections.content_summary: Two-direction statement: (A) ∫₀^∞ x^{n-1} F(x) dx can be found from the coefficient of x^n in F(x); (B) and conversely.

sections.title: A:- Proof of the Master Theorem
sections.content_summary: Ramanujan's formal proof: starts from ∫₀^∞ e^{-mx} x^{n-1} dx = Γ(n)/m^n, substitutes m = 1, r, r², ..., multiplies by Taylor-derivatives of f at a, and matches powers of x via Taylor expansion of f(a + hr^n) = φ(n).

sections.title: When valid? — convergence conditions
sections.content_summary: Four conditions: (a) F(x) Taylor-expansible; (b) F finite and continuous on (0,∞); (c) n > 0 (because the Eulerian integral requires it); (d) x^n F(x) vanishes at infinity.

sections.title: Generalization — substitution rules
sections.content_summary: Discusses substitutions: (a) any (α,β) → (0,∞) via (x-α)/(β-x)=y; (b) any transcendental can be reduced by substitution; (c) fractional powers handled by substitution.

sections.title: Example (i): ∫₀^∞ x^{m-1}/(1+x^n) dx = π/(n sin(πm/n))
sections.content_summary: Substitute x→y^{1/n}, then apply Master Theorem with φ(t)=Γ(1+t), get Γ(m/n)Γ(1-m/n) = π/sin(πm/n).

sections.title: Example (ii): Beta function ∫₀^1 x^{m-1}(1-x)^{n-1} dx = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m+n)
sections.content_summary: Substitute x→y/(1+y), apply Master Theorem with φ(t)=Γ(m+n+t)/Γ(m+n).

sections.title: Example (iii): ∫₀^∞ x^{n-1} cos(px) dx = Γ(n) cos(πn/2) / p^n
sections.content_summary: Substitute x→√y to turn cos px into alternating power series in y, apply Master Theorem with φ(t)=p^{2t}Γ(t+1)/Γ(2t+1). Derives sin version by differentiating in p.

sections.title: Example (iv): Bessel-function integral via Master Theorem
sections.content_summary: Substitute x→√y in a Bessel-style power series, apply Master Theorem to get a closed form in Γ functions.

sections.title: Example (v): ∫₀^∞ x^{n-1} dx / ∏_{k≥0}(1+a^k x) and triangular-number identity
sections.content_summary: Apply Master Theorem to the infinite product (1+x)(1+ax)(1+a²x)... Treats the product as a Taylor series 1 - A₁ x + A₂ x² - ... where A_r = 1/∏_{k=1}^r(1-a^k). Particular cases at n=1,2,3,1/2; the n=1/2 case gives an identity involving sum a^{n(n-1)/2} (triangular-number exponents).
sections.note: Surface notation involves a q-Pochhammer-like product. But Ramanujan does NOT use (a;q)_n notation, D_q, Heine, or the q-binomial theorem. He treats the product as an ordinary Taylor series in x and reduces to Master Theorem. So this does NOT trigger the schema's q_shift detector (correctly: the operator move is Master Theorem, not q-shift).

sections.title: Example (vi): ∫₀^∞ Γ(x+a)/(x^m Γ(x+a+n+1)) dx
sections.content_summary: Use Beta-function representation z^{x+a-1}(1-z)^n to land an integrand that is a Taylor series in x, apply Master Theorem with φ(t)=Γ(t+1)·(alternating ratios), final form involves csc(πm).

sections.title: B. Converse of A — Expansions of functions using the theorem
sections.content_summary: Statement: use Master Theorem in inverse direction to read off Taylor coefficients of F(x) from a known closed-form Mellin integral.

sections.title: B.(i): Expansion of (2/(1+√(1+4x)))^n
sections.content_summary: Substitution x = y+y², then y = z/(1-z), reduces to a Beta integral; reads off φ(p) = n·Γ(n-2p)/Γ(n-p+1), giving the explicit power-series coefficients (Catalan-numbers-style for n=1).
sections.note: This is functionally Lagrange inversion done via Master Theorem.

sections.title: B.(ii): Expansion of (x+√(1+x²))^{-n}
sections.content_summary: Substitution x + √(1+x²) = 1/y, then y = √(1-z²)... finally φ(p) = n·2^{p-1} Γ((n+p)/2)/Γ((n-p)/2+1), giving Chebyshev-style polynomial coefficients. Cor: change x→ix, n→in to get power series of e^{n·arcsin x}.

sections.title: B.(3): Given log x / x = -a, find expansion of x^n in powers of a
sections.content_summary: Substitute x → e^{-y}, apply Master Theorem with φ(p)=n(n+p)^{p-1}. Result: Lambert W / tree-function-style expansion.
sections.note: The φ(p)=n(n+p)^{p-1} formula is the Cayley tree formula / Lambert-W coefficients.

sections.title: B.(4): Given aq·x^p + x^q = 1, find expansion of x^n in powers of a
sections.content_summary: General algebraic-equation inversion via Master Theorem, giving φ(r) = n(n+pr-q)(n+pr-2q)...(n+pr-rq).
sections.note: This is the explicit power-series formula for a root of an algebraic equation in terms of the equation's coefficients — Lagrange inversion in its most general form, done via Master Theorem.

sections.title: Further example (a): ∫₀^∞ x^{r-1}(1-2mx/1!+3m²x²/2!-...) dx = Γ(r)(1-r)^m
sections.content_summary: Verifies at m=1, m=2 by direct computation; then exhibits the non-integer m=π case (which by then-known methods would be 'very difficult'). Cor: r=1/2, x→x² gives a √π evaluation.

sections.title: Further example (b): Expand e^{ax} in powers of e^{-bx} sin(cx)/c (Lagrange-like inversion)
sections.content_summary: Pulls e^{-ax} out as a Taylor series in y=e^{-bx} sinh(cx)/c; applies Master Theorem; uses Beta-integral reduction; final coefficient formula involves products like a(a-2b)(a²-3²c²)/3! etc.

sections.title: §2-§3: Convergence and validity discussion of (b)
sections.content_summary: Discusses when the expansion (b) is convergent; gives a closed-form bound e^{-(b/c) arctan(c/b)}/√(b²+c²).

sections.title: Particular cases (a)-(d) of (b)
sections.content_summary: (a) b=0 — gets e^{ax} = ∑ ... sin(cx)/c; (b) c=0 — gets Abel's theorem-style; (c) a→ai, b→bi — separates real and imaginary parts; (d) coefficient-of-a — gets x = ∑ ...e^{-kbx} sin(cx)/c.

sections.title: Roots of 1 - x³/3! + x⁶/6! - ... = 0 via cube roots of unity
sections.content_summary: Recognises 1 - x³/3! + x⁶/6! - ... = (e^{-x} + e^{-xω} + e^{-xω²})/3 where ω, ω² are primitive cube roots of unity. Reduces equation to (1/2)e^{-3x/2} cos(x√3/2) = -1/2. Approximates roots near πn/√3 (n odd) using a perturbation series in h = e^{-πn√3/2}.
sections.note: The multisection (∑_{n≡0 mod 3} x^{3n}/(3n)! extracted by averaging exp at 1, ω, ω²) is a distinct operator move. The 6-operator schema does not predict it. ChatGPT's broader taxonomy has FINITE_GAUSS_COLLAPSE which is the closest match.

sections.title: §4: Theorem II — Frullani-extended Master Theorem
sections.content_summary: Theorem II: if φ(0)=ψ(0) and φ(∞)=ψ(∞), then ∫₀^∞ (φ(ax)-ψ(bx))/x dx = [φ(0)-φ(∞)] log(b/a) + d/dn [log (n-th coefft of ψ / n-th coefft of φ)]_{n=0}. Proof takes n→0 limit in two Master-Theorem-derived integrals.
sections.note: The Frullani-limit move (n→0 in a Master-Theorem identity) is a distinct operator. The 6-operator schema does not capture this specific limit, though MASTER_THEOREM itself is the underlying primitive.

sections.title: §5: Examples of Theorem II — Frullani as special case
sections.content_summary: (1) Recovers Frullani's Theorem from φ=ψ; (2)-(4) various integrals involving (1+ax)^{-p} - (1+bx)^{-q} etc.; (5) multi-function generalization with p,q,r,s coefficients.

sections.title: §6: Corollaries (1)-(8) to Theorem I — cos/sin variants
sections.content_summary: (1) Cosine integral by substituting x→x², n→n/2, then un→un Γ(n/2)/Γ(n): get Γ(n) cos(πn/2). (2) πu_{-n}/sin(πn) version for n∈(0,1). (3)-(4) Variants for cos and arbitrary r. (5)-(8) Mixed product-integrals against cos nx.

sections.title: §7: Theorem III — Fourier cosine/sine self-reciprocity
sections.content_summary: Theorem III: if ∫₀^∞ φ(x) cos(nx) dx = ψ(n), then ∫₀^∞ ψ(x) cos(nx) dx = (π/2) φ(n). Same for sin.
sections.note: This is the Fourier cosine inversion theorem (modern: F_c·F_c = π/2·Id). It is NOT one of the 6 predicted operators. The 6-operator MELLIN_INVERSION is conceptually similar (continuous transform self-inverse) but the schema's regex looks for Mellin-specific signatures (x^{s-1}, Bromwich, Γ(s)) — Fourier cos has none of these.

sections.title: Examples of Theorem III + closing integrals
sections.content_summary: (1) ∫cos nx/(1+x²) dx = (π/2)e^{-n}. (2)-(3) ∫x^{p-1} e^{-ax} cos/sin nx dx with arctan(n/a) in the argument. (4) Gaussian cos integral, Fresnel-like ∫ cos(π/4 - a/x)/√x · cos nx dx = (√π/2√n) cos(2√(an)).

sections.title: §1: Validity of Theorem I revisited — nature of u_n
sections.content_summary: Notes that the theorem's validity depends on (a) n, (b) the function ∑(-1)^k u_k x^k/k!, and (c) the function u_n. Discusses continuity and finiteness conditions on u_n as a function of n.

sections.title: §2-§3: Uniqueness of the function passing through u_n
sections.content_summary: Argues there is one and only one 'unique' function passing through given values u_0, u_1, u_2, ... — modulo functions vanishing at all positive integers (such as sin(πn) or f(n)/Γ(-n)). Examples: u_n = n² is unique despite n² + sin²(πn) agreeing at integers.
sections.note: This is a meta-discussion about interpolation, important as a foundation for all subsequent fractional-iteration / fractional-differentiation work but not itself an operator move.

sections.title: §4-§5: Fractional Order of Functions — definition of F^n
sections.content_summary: Defines F^n(x) for non-integer n as the unique function passing through F^0, F^1, F^2, ... Example: F(x) = ax^p gives F^n(x) = a^{(p^n-1)/(p-1)} x^{p^n}; in particular F^{1/2}(x) = a^{1/(1+√p)} x^{√p}. Extends to irrational n via F^{√2}, F^{log 2}, F^e, F^π.
sections.note: This is the entry point to Ramanujan's fractional iteration theory. Closely related to the Schröder / Koenig functional equation tradition. Not in the 6-operator schema.

sections.title: §6: Conjugation theorem for fractional iteration + examples
sections.content_summary: Theorem: if F^m(x) = φ(x), F^n(x) = ψ(x), and f^m(x) = χ^{-1}φ(χ(x)), then f^n(x) = χ^{-1}ψ(χ(x)). Examples: (a) F(x) = (a(x^m+1)^p - 1)^{1/m}; (b) F(x) = x²-2 → F^n(x) via cosh-like closed form (Chebyshev family); (c) F^n for x²+2x, x²-2x, x²+4x; (d) iteration of x → (1-x)/(1-x²) involving F^{log 3}.
sections.note: Schröder conjugation: F^n acts on a fixed-point-free function by conjugating to a 'normal form' φ where the iterate is easy (a power map). Example (b) — F(x) = x²-2 has the Chebyshev semigroup as its iteration; F^{log 3/log 2}(x) = x³-3x and so on, which Ramanujan computes explicitly.

sections.title: §7: Orders of Infinity — Hardy ≺ notation
sections.content_summary: Adopts Hardy's ≺/≻ notation for asymptotic order comparison. Lists scales: x ≺ x² ≺ x³ ≺ ...; e^x ≻ x^x ≻ x! ≻ e^{x²} ≻ x^n (any n); e^x ≺ e^{e^x} ≺ e^{e^{e^x}}. Notes 'functions which defy all exponential scales'.

sections.title: §8: Construction of a function defying all logarithmic scales
sections.content_summary: Defines φ(x) by the functional equation xφ(x) = φ(log x), φ(0)=1. Computes φ(1)=1, φ(e)=1/e, φ(e^e)=1/e^{1+e}, .... Lets u_n = φ(tower of n e's); uses the 'unique function' to interpolate. Proves ∫₀^x φ dx grows like (log_n x) so the series ∑ φ(n) diverges, but sum to 10^{2,000,000} terms still doesn't exceed 5.

sections.title: §9: Scales of Orders of Infinity — theorem that the number of scales is infinite
sections.content_summary: Generalizes §8: given any 'scale' (a family closed under iteration of f), one can construct F by F(x) = f^{-1}(x) F(f(x)) such that ∫F defies that scale. Hence infinite tower of scales.

sections.title: §10: Expand f^r(x) in ascending powers of r — derives ψ_1(x) = C/F(x)
sections.content_summary: Taylor-expands f^r(x) = ψ_0(x) + r/1! ψ_1(x) + r²/2! ψ_2(x) + .... Shows ψ_0(x) = x, then by differentiating f^{r+h} = f^r∘f^h in two ways shows df^r/dr = ψ_1(x) df^r/dx, and ψ_n(x) = ψ_1(x) dψ_{n-1}/dx. Combined with §9 (∫F = const along f-orbit), deduces ψ_1(x) = C/F(x) — the infinitesimal generator of the iteration semigroup.
sections.note: This is the Lie-theoretic / generator-of-flow content of fractional iteration. Modern: ψ_1 is the vector field of the iteration flow.

sections.title: §11: Fractional Order of Differentiation
sections.content_summary: Defines D^n f(x) as the unique function passing through D^0, D^1, D^2, .... Theorem: ∫₀^∞ x^{n-1} f^{(r)}(a-x) dx = Γ(n) f^{(r-n)}(a). Use to define f^{(k)}(a) for non-integer k: pick r > k integer, set n = r-k, evaluate LHS. Cor: with n = 1/2, x → x²: ∫f(a-x²) dx = √π/2 · f^{(-1/2)}(a).
sections.note: This is the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative via the Cauchy formula, but with the role of f and its derivatives flipped (operates on f^{(r)}, returns f^{(r-n)}). Has a Mellin-style kernel x^{n-1} but is not what schema mellin_inversion detects; the schema looks for x^{s-1} F(x) where F is a function, not f^{(r)}.

sections.title: §12: The Use of Operators — shift E, difference Δ
sections.content_summary: Defines E = 1+Δ, E^n φ(0) = φ(n). Notes E^n φ(0) = φ(n) only when φ is the 'unique' function (§3). Example: Euler-Maclaurin sum formula derived heuristically. (ii) Conditions for substituting D (differentiation) for a scalar: result must be true for complex values. (iii) Example: substitute aD for a in Mellin formulas to get operator identities like ∫x^{n-1} ∑(-E)^s x^s/s! φ(0) dx = Γ(n)φ(-n) (recovers the Master Theorem with E acting on φ). Bessel-function example.
sections.note: Heaviside / umbral operator calculus. The MASTER_THEOREM appears here AS A CHECK / consistency test: substituting E for a scalar a in the Mellin integral gives back the Master Theorem statement. Methodologically interesting — Ramanujan is using the Master Theorem as a check on his operator calculus.

sections.title: §13: Partial fractions of an infinite product → cos integrals
sections.content_summary: Decomposes (1+x²/a²)(1+x²/(a+1)²)·...·(1+x²/(a+n)²)^{-1} as partial fractions in x²; takes n→∞ to get a series form. From this derives ∫₀^∞ cos(2nx) / ∏(1+x²/(a+k)²) dx = √π Γ(a+1/2)/[Γ(a) cosh^{2a}(n)]. Applies Theorem 12(b) to get ∫ cos(2nx)/cosh^{2a}(x) dx in inverse form.

sections.title: §14: Finite-vs-infinite Fourier — discontinuous-bandwidth theorem
sections.content_summary: Computes ∫₀^h e^{-ax} cos(mx) dx as real part of (1-e^{-(a+mi)b})/(a+mi). Combines with another integral to show: ∫₀^∞ ψ(x) cos(nx) dx = (π/2)φ(n) if n<h, = (π/4)φ(n) at n=h, = 0 if n>h, where ψ comes from ∫₀^h φ(x) cos(mx) dx.
sections.note: The bandlimited variant of Theorem III. This is essentially the Paley-Wiener phenomenon: compactly-supported φ has Fourier transform that 'looks band-pass' against trial functions.

sections.title: §15: Reciprocal-pair theorem — Mellin pair self-reciprocity + Bessel/Fourier corollaries
sections.content_summary: Theorem: if F and f satisfy ∫₀^∞ F(ax) f(bx) dx = 1/(a+b) (equivalently ∫x^{p-1} F dx · ∫x^{-p} f dx = π/sin(πp)), then the Fourier-like pair ψ(n) = ∫φ(x) [F(nxi)+F(-nxi)]/2 dx implies φ(n) = (2/π) ∫ψ(x)[f(nxi)+f(-nxi)]/2 dx. Corollaries: (1) e^{-x} pair gives Fourier cos pair (= Theorem III), (2) 1/(1+x²) pair, (3) Bessel J_n pair, (4) x → x^m variant, (5) m=n=2, a=b=1 gives ∫F(x²) dx · ∫f(x²) dx = π/4.
sections.note: Most general reciprocity theorem in the QRs. Uses MASTER_THEOREM in the proof (line 5234, line 5275) but the *operator* is Mellin-pair reciprocity — a generalization of Mellin self-inversion to pairs of functions.
